title: Reading a Robot Fleet Through Its Logs: Telemetry as a Diagnostic Instrument
excerpt: Bot activity logs are an under-exploited diagnostic surface. A field notes walkthrough of how Linux-side log analytics turned raw telemetry into predictive maintenance signals across a robotic fleet.

content.text: A warehouse robot fleet generates an extraordinary volume of passive telemetry — motor currents, encoder drift, battery curves, task latencies, fault codes. Most of it is written to logs and never read again. At GreyOrange, I started treating those logs as a *diagnostic instrument* rather than an audit trail, and the results reshaped how we approach predictive maintenance.
The Logs Were Already There

The first insight was almost embarrassingly simple: the data we needed already existed. Bot activity logs at scale — structured, timestamped, and machine-generated — are far cleaner than most "analytics datasets" people pay to acquire. The real work was not collection. It was **making the signal legible**.
Every diagnostic session started the same way on the Linux side: locate the log volume, understand the rotation policy, and reconstruct a timeline. A typical triage sequence looks like this:

content.code:
# Reconstruct a bot's day from rotated logs
zgrep -h "BOT-4471" /var/log/fleet/activity.log.*.gz \
  | awk -F'|' '{print $1, $4, $7}' \
  | sort > bot-4471-timeline.txt

# Fault-code frequency across the fleet (last 24h)
find /var/log/fleet -name "*.log" -mtime -1 -exec \
  grep -hoE "FAULT\[[A-Z_]+\]" {} \; \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

content.text: From Reactive to Predictive

The shift happened when we stopped asking "why did this bot fail?" and started asking "what did the telemetry look like in the hours *before* bots like this one failed?" That reframing turns log analytics from a forensic tool into a **predictive one**.

items: Encoder drift creep preceded mechanical faults by hours — early enough to schedule intervention during natural idle windows.
Battery voltage sag under load, not absolute charge, was the stronger predictor of mid-task stalls.
Task latency histograms separated network congestion from genuine compute exhaustion almost instantly — two faults that present identically to operators.

content.text: Observability is not about having more dashboards. It is about shortening the distance between a raw signal and a confident decision.
What I Would Tell My Past Self

content.title: Principle
content.text: Standardize the log schema before you scale the fleet, not after. Every hour spent retro-fitting structure onto unstructured logs is an hour of signal permanently lost to rotation.

The tooling does not need to be exotic. Linux utilities, a disciplined schema, and a habit of writing down what each signal *meant* in hindsight — that combination took the fleet from reactive firefighting to scheduled, evidence-driven maintenance.

title: Linux Tuning Lessons from the Field: Small Knobs, Measurable Throughput
excerpt: Systems optimization is rarely about heroic re-architecture. A collection of small, verified tuning decisions that compounded into measurable reliability gains on production machines.

content.text: There is a particular satisfaction in systems work: changing one line in a configuration file and watching a measurable metric move. Not guessed — **measured**. This post collects the tuning decisions that repeatedly earned their keep on production Linux machines.
Measure First, Tune Second

Every tuning session began with a baseline. `iostat`, `vmstat`, and `pidstat` formed the core loop — three tools, run for a full workload cycle, before touching anything. The number of "performance problems" that dissolved under a five-minute baseline review is remarkable.

content.code:
# Baseline: disk pressure + memory behavior across a full cycle
iostat -xz 5 12 > baseline-io.txt
vmstat 5 12 > baseline-vm.txt

# Who is actually waiting on I/O?
pidstat -d 5 | sort -k4 -rn | head

content.text: The Knobs That Paid for Themselves

items: **I/O scheduler selection** — switching throughput-oriented workloads from `cfq` to `deadline` eliminated latency spikes that no amount of application tuning had touched.
**Log rotation discipline** — uncompressed, unrotated logs were quietly becoming the fleet's largest I/O consumer. Rotation plus compression was the cheapest "upgrade" we ever shipped.
**vm.swappiness sanity** — the default of 60 was wrong for every telemetry node we ran. A conservative value kept hot pages in memory where they belonged.
**ulimit hygiene** — file descriptor ceilings set for a desktop world caused cascading failures exactly when load was highest.

content.text: Default configurations are designed to be safe everywhere, which means they are optimal almost nowhere.
The Compounding Effect

Individually, each of these is a small win. Together, they changed the character of the system: fewer stalls, fewer mystery slowdowns, and — critically — **telemetry that could be trusted**, because the logging path itself was no longer contending for the same resources it was measuring.

content.title: Takeaway
content.text: Optimization culture matters more than any single tuning value. Baseline, change one variable, re-measure, record. Repeat until the machine stops surprising you.

title: What 2.26 Million Loans Taught Me About Asking Better Questions
excerpt: The most valuable output of the consumer credit case study was not any single chart — it was a set of questions that survived contact with the data. Notes on analytical humility at scale.

content.text: Over a long analytical project on a 2.26-million-record consumer credit dataset, I learned that the difference between a competent analyst and a dangerous one is not SQL fluency. It is **the habit of interrogating your own conclusions** before anyone else gets the chance.
The Paradoxes Were the Real Deliverable

The headline findings were deliberately counter-intuitive: the *Volume vs. Risk Paradox* (the highest-volume loan category was not the highest-risk one), the *Income Insulation Myth* (high income did not proportionally protect against default), and the *Collateral Discrepancy* (renters defaulted at meaningfully higher rates than mortgage holders).
Each of these survived because it was attacked from multiple angles before it was presented:

items: **Segment re-slicing** — does the pattern hold across income brackets, vintages, and loan purposes independently?
**Denominator honesty** — are we comparing rates or raw counts, and does the choice flatter the conclusion?
**Survival bias checks** — is the dataset's "fully paid" population hiding loans too recent to have failed yet?

content.text: A finding that only appears in one slice of the data is not a finding. It is a hypothesis wearing a finding's clothes.
SQL as a Thinking Tool

Writing the aggregation queries forced clarity that no amount of staring at a dataframe provided. When you have to define an income bracket *in code* — with explicit boundaries and an explicit reason for them — vague thinking has nowhere to hide.

content.code:
-- Income tiers defined explicitly, not assumed
CASE
  WHEN annual_inc < 40000  THEN 'T1: <40K'
  WHEN annual_inc < 75000  THEN 'T2: 40-75K'
  WHEN annual_inc < 120000 THEN 'T3: 75-120K'
  ELSE 'T4: 120K+'
END AS income_tier

content.text: The Meta-Lesson

content.title: Takeaway
content.text: The dashboard was the least important artifact. The durable output was a mental checklist: define the denominator, attack the slice, name the bias, then — and only then — make the chart.
Data at scale does not reward confidence. It rewards **disciplined curiosity** — the willingness to let a beautiful hypothesis die under a clean query.
